content: Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with the use of nearly all antibacterial agents. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. The use of antibacterial agents disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which are responsible for the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may not respond to antimicrobial therapy and could require surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients who develop diarrhea following antibiotic use. A thorough medical history is essential, as CDAD has been reported to occur even two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Clinical management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic treatment for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation when indicated. Adequate hydration should be maintained either orally or, if required, via parenteral methods. As with other antibiotics, the use of Bacitracin may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi. If superinfection occurs, appropriate therapy should be initiated. Prescribing Bacitracin in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection, or without a prophylactic indication, is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. There have been reports of anaphylaxis and/or allergic contact dermatitis in patients exposed to Bacitracin for non-approved indications. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including Bacitracin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. They should not be used for viral infections, such as the common cold. When Bacitracin is prescribed for a bacterial infection, patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of treatment may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate therapy and increase the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance, making them untreatable by Bacitracin or other antibacterial drugs in the future. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even as late as two or more months after completing the last dose of the antibiotic. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician promptly.
